what_it_does.text: Makes many 2017-era individual tax cuts permanent, including lower rates, a larger standard deduction, and a higher alternative minimum tax exemption. It also raises the cap on deducting state and local taxes to $40,000 through 2029, then returns it to $10,000 in 2030.

Adds temporary deductions through 2028 for tips, overtime pay, new car loan interest, and a $6,000 deduction for people 65 and older. It also raises the child tax credit to $2,200 and expands child care credits and savings accounts.

Cuts SNAP in several ways. States would pay more of the administrative costs and, starting in 2028, part of the benefit costs if their error rates are high. Work rules tighten, eligibility narrows for some noncitizens, and benefit growth is limited to inflation.

Changes Medicaid for expansion adults, with work requirements, eligibility checks every six months, copays, and shorter retroactive coverage. It also caps state provider taxes and extra hospital payments, which could reduce the money states have for Medicaid.
Narrows health coverage and subsidies for many lawfully present immigrants in Medicaid, Medicare, and ACA marketplace plans. It also removes the repayment cap on excess marketplace subsidies.

Ends or shortens several clean energy tax credits, including those for home solar, home efficiency upgrades, EV chargers, clean vehicles, and wind and solar projects. It also expands business write-offs for equipment and research costs.

overview.district_bottom_line: Many households in this high-tax district would gain from the larger SALT cap, the permanent lower tax rates, and the expanded child and dependent care tax breaks. But the bill also puts pressure on New Jersey's budget through SNAP cost-sharing, Medicaid funding limits, and added health and food program rules, and it raises costs for residents who want solar or efficiency upgrades.

items.headline: SALT deduction cap rises from $10,000 to $40,000 through 2029
items.plain_english: For 2025 the cap on deducting state and local taxes goes from $10,000 to $40,000. It then rises 1% a year through 2029 and drops back to $10,000 in 2030. Households with income above $500,000 lose 30 cents of the higher cap for each dollar over that line, down to a $10,000 floor.

items.plain_english: The lower individual income tax rates set in 2017 were due to expire after 2025. This section removes the end date, so those rates continue for 2026 and later. It also changes how some brackets adjust for inflation, which can affect where higher brackets begin and end.

items.headline: Medicaid work requirements could cost some district adults their coverage
items.plain_english: Starting around January 2027, adults 19-64 in the Medicaid expansion group must show 80 hours a month of work, community service, job programs, or school, or meet an income test, or they can lose coverage. Many people are exempt, including parents of children 13 and under, people who are medically frail, and people already meeting SNAP work rules. Others could be dropped over paperwork or verification problems even if they qualify.

items.headline: Starting in 2028, New Jersey would pay part of SNAP food benefit costs
items.plain_english: Today the federal government pays the full cost of SNAP food benefits. Starting in fiscal year 2028, a state with a payment error rate of 6 percent or more would pay 5, 10, or 15 percent of benefit costs, depending on how high its rate is. A state under 6 percent would pay nothing. The most this section can do is leave New Jersey's costs unchanged, and otherwise it adds state costs that could pressure the state budget or the program.

items.headline: Child tax credit made permanent and raised to $2,200, with stricter SSN rules
items.plain_english: The $2,000 child tax credit would no longer expire after 2025, and it rises to $2,200 per child, with inflation adjustments after that. The refundable portion stays capped at $1,400, also adjusted for inflation. To claim the credit, a parent (at least one spouse on a joint return) and each child must have a Social Security number. That could cost some immigrant families the credit.
items.who_in_district: Families with children in this district's large middle- and upper-middle-income population gain from the higher, permanent credit, while families without the required Social Security numbers lose eligibility.

items.plain_english: Starting in fiscal year 2027, the federal government would pay 25% of what states spend to run SNAP instead of 50%. New Jersey would have to cover the other 25% or cut back on administration, which could mean slower processing or higher state and county costs. Benefits themselves are not changed by this section.

items.headline: Tightens SNAP work rules for adults and ends most local waivers
items.plain_english: This section rewrites who is exempt from SNAP work requirements. Parents are exempt only if their youngest child is under 14, and the exemption list no longer names veterans, homeless people, or former foster youth. It also limits the high-unemployment waivers to states outside the contiguous 48, so New Jersey could no longer ask for one. People who can't meet the work rules could lose food benefits.

items.headline: Medicaid expansion adults must reverify eligibility every six months, not yearly
items.plain_english: Starting with redeterminations scheduled after 2026, New Jersey must recheck eligibility every 6 months for adults covered under the Medicaid expansion. More frequent paperwork means some people who are still eligible may lose coverage because they miss a notice or can't submit documents in time. The section also gives $75,000,000 to federal Medicaid officials to carry out the change.
items.who_in_district: Low-income adults in the district's roughly 63,942 residents on Medicaid or other means-tested coverage, a share of whom are expansion adults, would face twice-yearly renewals.

items.headline: Caps extra Medicaid hospital payments, phased down over time for existing ones
items.plain_english: The bill limits the extra payments states direct to hospitals through Medicaid managed care plans. States that cover the expansion population (adults with low incomes) are capped at 100 percent of Medicare rates, and other states at 110 percent. Payments already approved before May 1, 2025 are kept at first, then cut by 10 percentage points a year starting in 2028 until they reach the cap. This could squeeze hospital finances over time, but the section does not say how much any hospital would lose.

items.headline: Caps and phases down state health-care taxes that help fund Medicaid
items.plain_english: States like New Jersey that expanded Medicaid currently can tax hospitals and other providers up to 6% of their patient revenue to help pay for Medicaid. Starting in fiscal year 2028, that ceiling drops by half a point a year to 3.5% in 2032, and states cannot add new taxes or raise existing ones. Nursing home and similar facility taxes are kept at their current level. With less of this money available, the state may have to cut Medicaid spending, including payments to providers, or find other money.
items.who_in_district: The 63,942 residents on Medicaid or other means-tested coverage, and the hospitals and other providers that serve them, are most exposed to any state cuts or funding gaps.

items.headline: Student loan repayment overhaul: safety net for some, tighter terms for others
items.plain_english: Starting in 2026, new federal loans can be repaid only through a fixed-term standard plan or a new income-based plan. That plan sets payments from 1% to 10% of income, with a $10 monthly minimum, a $50 reduction per dependent, and cancellation after 360 payments. Older income-contingent plans end by July 1, 2028, and parents' PLUS loans must use the standard plan with no income-based option.
items.who_in_district: Households with student or parent loans are affected, including higher earners who would pay up to 10% of income and lower-income borrowers who get the $10 minimum payment and interest relief.

items.headline: Overtime pay deduction helps some workers, but few in this high-income district
items.plain_english: From 2025 through 2028, workers can deduct the extra "half" part of legally required overtime pay, up to $12,500 ($25,000 for joint filers). The deduction shrinks for incomes above $150,000 ($300,000 joint) and requires a Social Security number and joint filing for married couples. It lowers taxes for eligible overtime earners but ends after 2028 and does not restore the SALT deduction.
items.who_in_district: Hourly and non-exempt workers, such as the 12.6% in service jobs, 18.1% in sales and office jobs, and 5.1% in construction and maintenance, are the most likely to benefit, while the 56.6% in management and professional jobs are mostly salaried and less likely to qualify.

items.headline: Temporary $6,000 senior deduction; personal exemptions stay at zero permanently
items.plain_english: The old personal exemption stays at zero permanently instead of returning after 2025. In its place, taxpayers 65 and older get a $6,000 deduction each for 2025 through 2028. That deduction shrinks as income rises above $75,000 for single filers or $150,000 for joint filers, and it requires a Social Security number on the return.
items.who_in_district: Seniors with modest or middle incomes get the clearest benefit, while higher-income seniors and larger families get little or nothing extra.

items.headline: Ends clean power credit for new wind and solar projects
items.plain_english: New wind and solar projects that start construction more than a year after enactment would lose the federal clean electricity tax credit if they are placed in service after 2027. The section also bars the credit for leased rooftop solar and adds strict rules on Chinese and other foreign-linked equipment and companies. It makes some nuclear projects easier to qualify, but that is a small offset for a district that has talked up solar as a way to grow its energy supply.
items.who_in_district: Homeowners considering rooftop solar, especially through a lease, and solar installers and developers would be most affected, while a small nuclear benefit is unlikely to reach many residents here.

items.headline: Limits SNAP to citizens, green card holders, and a few other groups
items.plain_english: This section narrows who can get SNAP to U.S. citizens and nationals, lawful permanent residents, Cuban and Haitian entrants, and people from certain Pacific island nations under Compact agreements. Other lawfully present noncitizens, such as refugees and asylees, would lose eligibility. Their income and resources would still count when figuring the benefit for the rest of their household, which could shrink benefits for mixed-status families.
items.who_in_district: The roughly 12,817 SNAP households in the district, especially immigrant families with refugees, asylees, or other noncitizens who would no longer qualify.

items.headline: Caps SNAP benefit growth to inflation, limiting future food-benefit increases
items.plain_english: This section ties SNAP benefits to the Thrifty Food Plan and allows only yearly inflation adjustments. Future re-evaluations of the food baskets, allowed no earlier than October 2027, cannot raise the plan's cost. SNAP benefits therefore cannot grow beyond inflation, even if a review finds that a healthy diet costs more.

items.headline: Makes the larger standard deduction permanent and raises it starting in 2025
items.plain_english: The bigger standard deduction from the 2017 tax law would have expired after 2025. This section keeps it permanently and raises it further, starting with the 2025 tax year. Households that take the standard deduction get more income shielded from federal tax. Homeowners with large property tax bills who itemize may gain less, because the standard deduction is now a higher bar to beat.
items.who_in_district: Most middle- and upper-middle-income households, including many retirees, would see a lower federal tax bill, while the many high-property-tax homeowners who itemize would see a smaller benefit.

items.plain_english: The 2017 limit on deducting interest for mortgages above $750,000 was due to expire after 2025. This section makes it permanent, so the old $1 million limit does not return. items.plain_english: Starting in 2026, families can claim a larger share of their child and dependent care costs as a tax credit. The top rate is 50 percent for lower incomes, and it stays at 35 percent or higher until income passes $75,000 ($150,000 for joint filers). Above that it phases down, but never below 20 percent.
items.who_in_district: Middle- and upper-middle-income working families with kids or dependents needing care, including many two-earner couples near the district's $130,387 median income, would see a larger credit.

items.plain_english: The bill cuts off the homeowner tax credit for things like rooftop solar for any spending after December 31, 2025. The credit would otherwise have run through 2034 and is now 30 percent. Homeowners who install after that date lose the credit, which makes these upgrades more expensive for them.

items.plain_english: The bill ends the clean electricity investment credit for wind and solar projects that come online after 2027 and bars the credit for projects with material help from certain foreign entities. It also denies the credit for rooftop solar and similar property that is leased to a third party. Energy storage is exempt from the wind and solar cutoff, and fuel cells get a 30 percent credit.
items.who_in_district: Homeowners considering leased rooftop solar and developers of solar projects in the district would face higher costs, while battery storage projects keep the credit.

items.plain_english: Starting October 1, 2026, the federal government would pay a state's Medicaid and CHIP costs only for citizens, green card holders, Cuban and Haitian entrants, and people living here under Compacts of Free Association. Lawfully present immigrants in other categories would no longer be covered by federal funds, so New Jersey would have to pay their costs itself or end their coverage. The section references some exceptions but does not spell them out.

items.headline: Keeps higher AMT exemption permanent, sparing many high-tax households a second tax calculation
items.plain_english: The alternative minimum tax is a parallel tax calculation that can raise bills for households with large deductions, such as state and local taxes. This section makes the higher exemption levels from the 2017 tax law permanent instead of letting them lapse after 2025. Fewer households would owe the extra tax as a result. The phaseout rate also doubles to 50 percent for the very highest earners, so they lose the exemption faster, though the phaseout starts at a much higher income level.
items.who_in_district: Higher-earning homeowners with large property tax bills benefit most, while only households with very high incomes would lose exemption value from the faster phaseout.

items.headline: Pass-through business owners keep a bigger tax deduction, with a $400 minimum
items.plain_english: The section widens the phase-in range for the pass-through business income deduction, so more owners of higher-earning businesses can keep more of it. It also sets a minimum deduction of $400 for owners who actively work in a business and earn at least $1,000 of business income. Both changes start with tax year 2026.

items.headline: Companies can again deduct U.S. research costs immediately, benefiting NJ-5's professional economy
items.plain_english: The section lets businesses deduct U.S.-based research and software development costs in the year they spend the money, instead of spreading them over five years. It starts with 2025 tax years. Smaller businesses can apply it retroactively to 2022 and amend past returns. Research done overseas still has to be written off over 15 years.
items.who_in_district: Employers and workers in research-, software-, and management-heavy fields, plus small businesses that invest in development, would see the most direct benefit.

items.headline: New 0.5%-of-income floor trims charitable deductions for itemizing donors
items.plain_english: Starting in 2026, people who itemize could deduct charitable gifts only to the extent they exceed 0.5 percent of their income base. The first slice of giving would no longer count, so taxes would rise slightly for donors. The section also makes technical changes to the cash-gift limit and the carryover rules for gifts that can't be deducted in a given year.
items.who_in_district: Higher-income, itemizing homeowners and older donors who give regularly to charities, churches and nonprofits would be affected most, while households that take the standard deduction would see little change.

items.headline: Tipped workers can deduct up to $25,000 of tips through 2028
items.plain_english: Workers in jobs that customarily get tips can deduct up to $25,000 a year of cash tips from their taxable income, even if they don't itemize. The deduction shrinks for higher earners (starting at $150,000, or $300,000 for joint filers) and ends after 2028. Married couples must file jointly, a Social Security number is required, and tips earned in certain professional service businesses don't count.
items.who_in_district: Servers, bartenders, salon workers, and delivery drivers in the district's 12.6% service-occupation workforce would benefit, while the 56.6% of workers in management and professional jobs are mostly unaffected.

items.headline: Medicaid expansion adults above poverty line face required copays starting 2028
items.plain_english: Starting October 1, 2028, states must charge copays to expansion adults with incomes above the poverty line, up to $35 per service. Primary care, mental health, substance use care, and community health center visits are exempt. Total cost sharing is capped at 5 percent of family income, and providers may refuse care if the copay isn't paid.

items.plain_english: This section lets businesses deduct the full cost of qualifying equipment and other eligible property in the year they buy it, with no phase-down, for property acquired after January 19, 2025. Businesses that invest in equipment can lower their tax bills, which fits the lower-taxes message. It does nothing for the SALT deduction, and it mainly helps owners and firms that buy equipment, not wage earners or households.

items.plain_english: The section bars HHS from putting in place, running, or enforcing the 2024 federal minimum staffing rule for nursing homes until September 30, 2034. Nursing homes avoid the cost and hiring burden of the mandate. Residents and families lose the added staffing requirements the rule would have set.

items.plain_english: Medicare enrollment would be restricted to U.S. citizens, green card holders, Cuban and Haitian entrants, and certain residents from Pacific island nations with Compact of Free Association agreements. People already on Medicare who do not fit those groups would lose coverage 18 months after enactment. Social Security would review current enrollees within a year and send notices to those affected.

items.plain_english: Starting in 2027, only green card holders, Cuban and Haitian entrants, and people living here under Compact of Free Association agreements could get ACA premium subsidies. Other legally present immigrants, such as refugees and asylees, would lose eligibility and could face much higher premiums or go uninsured. The section also adds immigration-status checks to the marketplace sign-up process.

items.plain_english: The section raises what Medicare pays doctors and other clinicians under the physician fee schedule by 2.5 percent for services in 2026 only. items.plain_english: This section ends the tax credit for energy-efficient home improvements, such as qualifying furnaces, boilers, and other upgrades, for property placed in service after December 31, 2025. Under current law the credit would have run through 2032. Homeowners who plan upgrades in 2026 or later would lose a tax break that lowers what they pay for these projects.

items.headline: New car loan interest becomes deductible for most district households through 2028
items.plain_english: For 2025 through 2028, buyers can deduct up to $10,000 a year in interest on a loan for a new, U.S.-assembled personal vehicle, even if they don't itemize. The deduction shrinks by $200 for every $1,000 of income above $100,000 ($200,000 for joint filers) and ends entirely at higher incomes. items.plain_english: Workers whose employers offer a dependent care assistance program can set aside up to $7,500 tax-free for child or dependent care, up from $5,000. The limit for married people filing separately rises from $2,500 to $3,750. It starts in tax years after December 31, 2025.

items.plain_english: Families can use 529 accounts tax-free for more K-12 costs, such as books, curriculum, tutoring, test fees, dual enrollment and therapies for students with disabilities. The yearly limit on K-12 spending from these accounts doubles from $10,000 to $20,000 starting in 2026. items.headline: New $1,700 credit for school scholarship donations, only if New Jersey opts in
items.plain_english: Starting in 2027, individuals who give cash to approved scholarship groups could claim a federal tax credit of up to $1,700 a year. The credit is reduced by any state credit for the same gift, and the gift cannot also be deducted as a charitable contribution. Scholarships go to students from households earning up to 300 percent of area median income and can cover K-12 school expenses. The scholarship money is not taxed to the family. items.plain_english: This section blocks the federal government from putting into effect a 2023 rule meant to make it easier and faster for low-income Medicare beneficiaries to enroll in Medicare Savings Programs, which help pay Medicare premiums. This section removes that cap, so anyone whose income came in higher than estimated would owe back the full excess at tax time. It applies starting with the 2026 tax year.

The point at which that deduction starts to phase out rises from $2,500,000 to $4,000,000. items.plain_english: The bill lets investors in qualifying small companies exclude more of their gain from tax. promise_alerts.explanation: The commitment was to fight to protect programs Jersey families depend on, and H.R. 1 makes cuts to several of them. It adds Medicaid work requirements (71119) and six-month reverification (71107). It phases down state provider taxes (71115) and shifts SNAP benefit and administrative costs to New Jersey (10105, 10106). It also tightens SNAP work rules and eligibility (10102, 10108). The bill does include offsets such as a higher SALT cap, a larger child tax credit, and expanded child care credits, but these are tax provisions and do not protect the Medicaid and SNAP programs it cuts.

The pledge was about the 2021 Build Back Better reconciliation package, not this bill, so it does not clearly cover this vote. The bill only partly restores SALT. It raises the cap from $10,000 to $40,000 for 2025 and rises 1% a year through 2029, phases the higher cap down for households above $500,000, and returns it to $10,000 in 2030. It does not repeal the cap, and it separately trims itemized deductions for top-bracket filers. Whether this counts as "reinstating SALT" depends on how the pledge is read and whether it carries over to a different package.

The bill changes the tax code in ways that affect families, and the pledge ties support to reinstating SALT. Section 70120 raises the cap from $10,000 to $40,000, but only through 2029. The cap reverts to $10,000 in 2030, and it phases down for households earning over $500,000. Whether that counts as 'reinstating SALT' or falls short of a full restoration depends on how the pledge is read. The pledge was also made in 2021, not about this bill.

The commitment calls an earlier SALT increase a "down payment" toward fully restoring the deduction in 2025. Section 70120 raises the cap from $10,000 to $40,000 for 2025, but it does not restore the full deduction. It phases the higher cap down for households above $500,000 of income, applies a 1% annual increase through 2029, and returns the cap to $10,000 in 2030. Because the bill's 2025 outcome is a capped, partial deduction, it falls short of the stated goal of full restoration.

The commitment is a general statement about the House-passed H.R. 1, with three parts: cut taxes, lower costs, and don't abandon seniors and hungry children. The bill does cut taxes, including the higher SALT cap, permanent 2017 rates, and a larger standard deduction. It also makes SNAP changes (state cost-sharing, tighter work rules, a benefit-growth cap, narrower immigrant eligibility), Medicaid changes (work requirements, six-month rechecks, provider-tax limits), and a cut to Medicare eligibility for some immigrants. Whether this conflicts depends on how one reads "abandon vulnerable seniors and hungry children," since the commitment names no specific provision or vote.

The commitment says the House-passed H.R. 1 "defunds key investments in alternative energy, including solar projects." The findings support this. Section 70512 ends the clean electricity credit for new solar and wind projects placed in service after 2027 and bars it for leased rooftop solar. Section 70513 does the same, and section 70506 ends the homeowner solar credit after 2025. The bill does keep or add some energy credits (storage, fuel cells, some nuclear), but these do not offset the solar cuts. "Defunds" is loose wording for ending tax credits rather than cutting appropriations.

The commitment is a general pledge to fight for lower taxes for families and small businesses and to make life more affordable. The bill meets the tax half: it makes the 2017 rates and the larger standard deduction permanent, raises the SALT cap to $40,000, raises the child tax credit to $2,200, and expands small-business expensing and the pass-through deduction. On affordability, it also adds costs and cuts for many households, including SNAP cost-sharing and tighter work rules, Medicaid work requirements and copays, the end of several energy credits, and an uncapped repayment of excess ACA subsidies. Whether it conflicts depends on how broadly "affordable" is read, because the commitment is not tied to any specific provision.

The commitment is a broad campaign slogan about "lower taxes" and "Jersey Values", not a pledge about a specific vote. The bill does lower taxes in many ways: the SALT cap rises to $40,000 through 2029, the 2017 rates and the larger standard deduction become permanent, and the child tax credit is raised. It also cuts Medicaid and SNAP, ends clean energy credits, and shifts costs onto New Jersey, so whether it conflicts depends on what "Jersey Values" means and how the tax cuts are weighed against those cuts.
